extracted.intended_audience: War Department officials, pension adjudicators, military lawyers, and administrators handling military claims and veterans' benefits
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and administrative rules for deciding whether injury, disease, death, or disability was incurred 'in the line of duty' (for pensions, artificial limbs, and related benefits), plus related rules on passes, furloughs, confinement, detail of officers, and issue/return of ordnance to institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pass duration and status for line-of-duty
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an essential incident in the operation of a 'pass' that the permission to be absent should not be for more than 24 hours, i.e., for such a length of time as to operate to remove the soldier from the possibility of being called for the performance of the more important duties for which he is expected to hold himself in constant readiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men on pass are not removed from the list of those who are 'present for duty' on the rolls; a man on pass who is in the immediate neighborhood of the post and subject to call is, in the general case, in line of duty. To regard such a man as 'absent with leave' or 'on furlough' would work a serious injury to his status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of absence determined by duration/status not name
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of the instrument with regard to 'line of duty', in the operation of which the soldier absents himself, should be determined by the duration of the absence and the status created rather than by its name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'hunting passes' provided in Army Regulations (privileges for hunting as instruction in small-arms practice) fall within the description of duty for injuries received while so engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized acts may negate line-of-duty status
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a soldier is in a status of duty, an act that is unauthorized can render the resulting disability not incurred in the line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: An enlisted man on pass for bathing who discharged a borrowed rifle and was injured — though in a status of duty, the act was unauthorized and the resulting disability was not incurred in line of duty (C. 2658, Mar. 25, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Furloughs can be in line of duty in certain circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier when on furlough may be in line of duty as when en route to his station, or when during his furlough he is, in compliance with orders, on his way to a place to report his whereabouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being on furlough does not automatically exclude line-of-duty status; context such as being en route under orders matters (C. 2658, Oct. 15, 1896).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad statutory meaning of 'in the line of duty' for pensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The term employed in the pension laws — 'in the line of duty' — is much more comprehensive than the term 'on duty' as used in the thirty-eighth article of war; its application is not limited to actual present performance of a specific military duty but relates to a condition under which military duty may regularly be performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pension laws being beneficial in character, the term is to be construed so as to advance the benefit rather than to restrict it. (Citations: R. 41, 2 Op. Atty. Gen. opinions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory negligence/gross carelessness affects pension entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross carelessness by a soldier renders his title to a pension from an injury resulting from such carelessness questionable on the ground of contributory negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative rulings have denied pensionable status where the soldier's recklessness is a culpable contributing cause (C. 2474, Aug. 3, 1896).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infraction of discipline excludes duty-performance injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an incident (e.g., a scuffle between soldiers) is an infraction of military discipline within the meaning of relevant articles of war, injuries resulting therefrom are not considered incurred in the performance of military duty for pension purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple decisions hold such injuries not pensionable (e.g., J. 13017, July 25, 1902; P. 58, Feb. 8, 1893).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor infractions may not bar line-of-duty if not culpable negligence
rubrics_metrics.description: An infraction of discipline that is not of such degree as to amount to culpable contributory negligence does not prevent a disability from being regarded as incurred in the line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Soldier left reservation to mail a personal letter, was frozen and permanently disabled — infraction not so grave; disability held in line of duty (G. 13077, Aug. 26, 1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental injury while preparing for special duty can be pensionable
rubrics_metrics.description: An accidental wound caused by the discharge of a weapon while the soldier was engaged in cleaning it for use in the performance of special duty, being unattended by contributory negligence, was in the line of duty for pensionable purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that preparatory acts for performance of ordered duty may be protected if no contributory negligence (G. 2474, Aug. 3, 1896).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confinement (punishment) does not automatically remove line-of-duty status
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a part of military duty to submit to punishment; a soldier is not necessarily out of the line of duty when in confinement, and if an injury received during confinement was a casualty of the service not incurred by his own fault, his pension claim should not be prejudiced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities support pension allowance where confinement-related injuries are not due to the soldier's own negligence or fault (R. 41, 2 Op. Atty. Gen.; G. 3063; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory locations/conditions may exclude line-of-duty for furlough injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 4694, R. S., a disability incurred while on furlough is not in the line of duty for pensionable purposes if the soldier was not, at the time, in the field, on the march, at a post, fort, or garrison, or en route by direction of competent authority to some post, fort, or garrison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific statute-limited situations can categorically exclude pensionability (C. 13357, Sept. 29, 1902; 26919, June 23, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sick furloughs and veteran furloughs treated as line-of-duty
rubrics_metrics.description: An enlisted man absent from his command on sick furlough remained 'in the line of duty'; similarly, section 4700 puts enlisted men on veteran furlough with their organization upon the same footing as men on sick furlough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Volunteer soldier on sick furlough disabled by a horse kick before furlough expiration was held to be in line of duty for certain statutory acts (P. 441, Jan., 1891).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney General Cushing definition favorable to pension claimants
rubrics_metrics.description: Cushing's definition: 'He who contracts disease or dies in consequence of the ordinary performance of his military duty, or in the performance of any special act of military duty, whether at the moment of performance he was on duty or off duty...contracts it "in the line of duty."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expansive, benefit-favoring definition has been accepted as the meaning invested by statutes and used to guide pension administration (7 Op. Atty. Gen., 161; cited repeatedly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior Department discretion in line-of-duty determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Interior Department ordinarily decides for itself whether, for pension purposes, a death or disability was incurred in the line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative agencies exercise factfinding discretion in each claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgeon General authority for artificial limbs under section 4787
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4787, R. S., and related acts provide that artificial limbs shall be issued in cases of injury in line of duty; the Surgeon General is specifically designated as the authority to pass on the question of whether the disability was incurred in line of duty for this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions: C. 2221, Dec. 16, 1908 and Jan. 16, 1909. Also, Surgeon General's regulations are auxiliary to the statute and do not divest persons of rights to prosecute claims (R. 49, 225, July, 1885).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Hired men of the land forces' includes certain mechanics/laborers
rubrics_metrics.description: The description 'hired men of the land forces' in the act of February 27, 1877, may be properly construed to include mechanics and laborers employed at arsenals by authority of provisions of Title XVII of the Revised Statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant to eligibility for benefits under the artificial-limb statutes (R. 39, 316, Nov., 1877).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triennial entitlement rules for artificial limbs (effect of 1891 act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the amending act of March 3, 1891, persons entitled to be furnished artificial limbs whose cases had three or more years (and less than five) elapsed since their last legal receipt became entitled to receive at once a new limb, and thereafter at triennial intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The act was prospective; earlier quinquennial rights could not be revised retroactively; provisions about payment in lieu of limbs still apply to triennial rights (P. 44, Mar., 1891).

rubrics_metrics.name: General limitation: disability must not result from unlawful/unauthorized act
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation recognized in practice is that the disability must not be the result of the unlawful or unauthorized act as a direct or contributory cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle modifies earlier stricter constructions and accords with the legislative intent to confer benefits except where the soldier's own unlawful conduct materially caused the disability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1225 detail-of-officers: 'established' institutions only
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act authorizing detail of officers and issue of arms to colleges, the term 'established' is to be interpreted as including incorporated institutions or those established by law (State institutions); an unincorporated private school is not 'established' for this statute's purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, officers and ordnance are properly detailed/issued only to qualifying institutions; prior ad hoc issuances (e.g., Washington High School, 1885) were later questioned unless backed by specific authorization (P. 6x, Apr., 1894; other citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical and duration limits on officer details to colleges
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory acts set numeric limits (total number of officers to be detailed) and restrict detail tours to four years (Act Nov. 3, 1893); the period described is the length of a detail, and reassignment requires formal relief and re-detailing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reassignment to a second detail requires relieving the officer from college duty and issuing new orders; frequency and interval between details are determined by the Secretary of War if not statutorily provided (C. 13791, Dec. 12, 1902).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War authority to issue arms to colleges where officer detailed
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War is authorized to issue arms to any college where an Army or Navy officer has been detailed under section 1225, R.S.; requisitions for such ordnance require approval of the governor of the State or Territory in which the college is located.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative practice limits issuance to institutions with regularly detailed officers and requires appropriate approvals (P. 38, 201, Jan., 1890; G. 18007, Jan. 21, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Custody and returns for ordnance entrusted to institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The official of the college to whom ordnance stores are intrusted may be required to render returns as indicated in section 1167, R.S., directing that all 'officers, agents or persons' receiving ordnance stores make certain regular returns according to prescribed forms and rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to render returns or damage through carelessness may expose the institution to suit on bond or direct suit against the owners; demands for return of ordnance must be signed by Chief of Ordnance by authority of the Secretary of War (R. 4x, May, 1879; G. 2902; other citations).
